source_text: Συλλογισάμενος οὖν τά τε σοφίας ἀγαθά, καὶ τὰ ἀφροσύνης κακά, εἰκότως ἂν ἱκανῶς θαυμάζοιμι ἄνδρα τοιοῦτον, ὅς τις φερόμενος ἀλόγως· ἔπειτα ἑαυτοῦ λαβόμενος, εἰς τὸ δέον ἐπιστρέψει. Φρονήσεως γὰρ καὶ ἀφροσύνης πολὺ τὸ μέσον, διαφορὰ δὲ ἀμφοῖν τοσαύτη, ὅση περ ἡμέρας πρὸς νύκτα. Ἔοικε τοίνυν, ὁ μὲν ἀρετὴν ᾑρημένος, τρανῶς τε ἕκαστα καὶ ἄνω βλέποντι· τῆς τε ἑαυτοῦ πορείας, λαμπροτάτου φέγγους καιρῷ πεποιημένῳ· ὁ δ᾽ αὖ κακίᾳ ἐμπεπλεγμένος, καὶ πλάνῃ παντοίᾳ ὡς ἐν σκοτομήνῃ πλανωμένῳ, τυφλός τε ὢν τὴν πρόσοψιν, καὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ σκότους τῶν πραγμάτων ἀφῃρημένος. Τέλος δὲ ἐπινοήσας ἑκατέρου τῶν βίων τούτων ἐγὼ τὸ διάφορον, εὗρον οὐδέν, καὶ ὡς κοινωνὸν ἀφρόνων ἐμαυτὸν καταστήσας, τὰ τῆς ἀφροσύνης ἐπίχειρα δέξομαι. Τί γὰρ ἢ τῶν σοφισμάτων ἐκείνων ἀγαθόν, ἢ ποία ὄνησις τῶν πολλῶν λόγων, ὅπου γε τὰ φλυαρίας ῥεύματα, ὥσπερ ἐκ πηγῆς ὁρμᾶται τῆς ἀφροσύνης; Σοφῷ δὲ καὶ ἄφρονι κοινὸν οὐδέν, οὐ κατὰ ἀνθρώπων μνήμην, οὐ κατὰ Θεοῦ ἀμοιβήν. Τῶν δ᾽ ἐν ἀνθρώποις πραγμάτων, ἔτι ἄρχεσθαι δοκούντων, ἤδη τὸ τέλος ἐπιλαμβάνει ἁπάντων. Σοφὸς δὲ οὐδέποτε ἀσυνέτῳ τοῦ αὐτοῦ κοινωνεῖ τέλους. Ἐμίσησα τοίνυν καὶ τὸν σύμπαντά μου βίον, τὸν ἐν τοῖς ματαίοις ἀναλωθέντα, ὃν διήγαγον τοῖς περὶ γῆν πόνοις προστετηκώς. Ὡς γὰρ συνελόντι φάναι, πάντα μοι λυπηρῶς ἐκμεμόχθηται ὁρμῆς ἀλογίστου γενόμενα ποιήματα· καὶ διαδέξεταί τις αὐτὰ ἕτερος, εἴτε σοφός, εἴτε ἠλίθιος, τὰς ψυχρὰς τῶν ἐμῶν καμάτων ἐπικαρπίας. Ἀπολαβομένῳ δέ μοι ταῦτα καὶ ἀπορρίψαντι, κατεφάνη τὰ τῷ ὄντι ἀγαθὰ προκείμενα ἀνθρώπῳ, σοφίας τε γνῶσις, καὶ κτῆσις ἀνδρείας. Εἰ δέ τις τούτων μὲν οὐκ ἐφρόντισεν, ἑτέρων δὲ ἐπτόηται, ὁ τοιοῦτος εἵλετο μὲν πονηρὰ ἀντὶ ἀγαθῶν, μετῆλθε δὲ κακίαν ἀντὶ χρηστότητος, καὶ μόχθον ἀνθ᾽ ἡσυχίας, ταράχοις ποικίλοις περιελκόμενος, νύκτωρ τε καὶ μεθ᾽ ἡμέραν συνεχόμενος ἀεί, σώματός τε ἐπείγουσι καμάτοις, καὶ ψυχῆς φροντίσιν ἀδιαλείπτοις, σφαδαζούσης αὐτῷ τῆς καρδίας, ἀλλοκότων ἕνεκα πραγμάτων. Οὐ γὰρ τὸ τέλειον ἀγαθὸν περὶ βρῶσίν τε καὶ πόσιν ἱζάνει· εἰ καὶ μάλιστα ἐκ Θεοῦ ἀνθρώποις γίνονται αἱ τροφαί· οὐδὲν γὰρ τῶν πρὸς σωτηρίαν ἡμῖν δεδομένων ἔξω τῆς αὐτοῦ ὑπάρχει προνοίας. Ἀλλ᾽ ὁ μὲν ἀγαθὸς ἀνήρ, σοφίας ἐκ Θεοῦ τυχών, εὐφροσύνης ἔτυχεν οὐρανίου· ὁ δ᾽ αὖ πονηρός, θεηλάτοις ἐλαυνόμενος κακοῖς, πλεονεξίαν νοσῶν, πολλά τε ἀθροῖσαι σπουδάζει, καὶ τὸν ὑπὸ Θεοῦ τετιμημένον ἐναντίον τοῦ πάντων Δεσπότου ὀνειδίσαι σπεύδει, δῶρα προτείνων ἄχρηστα, δολερά τε ὁμοῦ καὶ μάταια τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἀθλίας ψυχῆς σπουδάσματα πεποιημένος.
thought_title: Solomon weighs wisdom against folly, finds life in vanity grievous, and discerns the true good
orientation: Solomon reflects on his own experience, comparing the man who chooses virtue with the man entangled in vice, and concludes that all his toil under the sun has been sorrowful and empty, so that the true goods set before humanity are knowledge of wisdom and possession of courage, which come from God.

lemmas.gloss: having reasoned, having concluded by reasoning
is carried, is borne along (here: carried unreasonably)
taking hold of himself, recovering himself

choices.why: Captures the deliberative weighing of wisdom and folly that precedes the judgment; 'reflecting' would weaken the logical force.
Preserves the passive motion of a man swept along by unreason; 'walking' or 'behaving' loses the image of being borne.
The noun denotes thick darkness or gloom; 'gloom' is possible but 'darkness' matches the stark day/night contrast just made.
Glossary fixes 'idle talk' for φλυαρία; 'streams' keeps the spring metaphor intact.
In this context 'courage' is the virtue paired with wisdom; 'manliness' is too gendered, 'fortitude' is acceptable but 'courage' is plainer.
Means 'impious' or 'hated by God'; 'godless' fits the antithesis to the good man who receives wisdom from God.

bible_refs.note: ἐκκλησιάζων ... φλυαρίας ῥεύματα / 'streams of idle talk' echoes the Preacher's pursuit of folly and madness
ἐμίσησα ... τὸν βίον / 'I hated ... my life' matches the Preacher's hatred of life under the sun
διαδέξεταί τις αὐτὰ ἕτερος / 'another shall inherit them' reflects the Preacher's grief that his toil goes to a successor, wise or foolish
οὐ τὸ τέλειον ἀγαθὸν περὶ βρῶσίν τε καὶ πόσιν ἱζάνει / 'the perfect good does not sit about eating and drinking' parallels the Preacher's statement that enjoyment comes from God
σοφίας ἐκ Θεοῦ τυχών / 'obtaining wisdom from God' reflects the Preacher's search for wisdom that is far off and deep

pass_b_english: Having reasoned through both the goods of wisdom and the evils of folly, I would rightly marvel at a person who is carried along unreasonably, then recovers himself and turns to what is proper. For the distance between prudence and folly is vast, the difference between them as great as day compared to night. The one who has chosen virtue resembles a man who sees each thing clearly and upward, his own course made in the season of brightest light; but the one entangled in vice, wandering in every kind of error as if in thick darkness, is blind in his outlook and cut off by the darkness of things. Finally, having devised the distinction between these two lives, I found nothing, and making myself a companion of fools I will receive the wages of folly. For what good is there from those sophistries, or what benefit from many words, when streams of idle talk surge forth as from a spring of folly? A wise person and a fool share nothing in common, neither according to human memory nor according to God's recompense. As for the affairs among humans, even while they seem to be just beginning, the end already seizes hold of them all. A wise person never shares the same end as one who lacks understanding. Therefore I hated even my whole life, the one consumed in empty things, which I passed burdened with toils upon the earth. For to put it concisely, everything has been painfully wrought for me as works of an unreasoning impulse; and someone else will inherit them, whether wise or foolish, reaping the cold fruits of my labors. Having received these things and cast them away, the truly good things set before a human being appeared to me: the knowledge of wisdom, and the possession of courage. But if someone has not attended to these, yet is infatuated with other things, such a person has chosen evils instead of goods, pursued vice instead of goodness, and toil instead of quiet, dragged along by varied disturbances, oppressed continually both night and day, by the body's pressing fatigue and the soul's unceasing anxieties, his heart fluttering because of alien matters. For the perfect good does not sit around eating and drinking; even if nourishment comes to humans especially from God, nothing of what is given to us for salvation lies outside his own providence. But the good man, obtaining wisdom from God, gains heavenly joy; whereas the wicked man, driven on by evils sent from God, sick with greed, strives to amass many things and hastens to insult the one honored by God before the Lord of all, offering useless gifts, making his own wretched pursuits both deceitful and empty.

problems.why: θεηλάτοις means 'God-driven/sent by God'. The evils are inflicted by God, not 'godless'. The sense is reversed.
problems.fix: driven on by evils sent from God

problems.quote: exchanged vice for kindness, and toil for quiet
problems.source_quote: μετῆλθε δὲ κακίαν ἀντὶ χρηστότητος, καὶ μόχθον ἀνθ᾽ ἡσυχίας
problems.why: The ἀντί phrases mean he pursued vice instead of goodness and toil instead of rest. The English reads as trading vice and toil away for kindness and quiet.
problems.fix: pursued vice instead of goodness, and toil instead of quiet

problems.quote: I will accept the undertakings of folly
problems.why: ἐπίχειρα means wages or reward. 'Undertakings' loses the idea of receiving folly's payment.
problems.fix: I will receive the wages of folly

problems.quote: yet is terrified by other things
problems.why: ἐπτόηται with the genitive means he is excitedly taken up with other things, not frightened by them.
problems.fix: yet is infatuated with other things
problems.ruling: ἐπτόηται (πτοέω) here means being stirred or infatuated with 'other things' (ἑτέρων), set against 'not cared for these'. 'Terrified' wrongly makes it fear.

problems.quote: So it appears: the one who chooses virtue looks at everything clearly and upward, his own path illumined by the brightest light at the appointed time
problems.source_quote: Ἔοικε τοίνυν, ὁ μὲν ἀρετὴν ᾑρημένος, τρανῶς τε ἕκαστα καὶ ἄνω βλέποντι· τῆς τε ἑαυτοῦ πορείας, λαμπροτάτου φέγγους καιρῷ πεποιημένῳ
problems.why: ἔοικε means he resembles one who looks upward; the course is made in a season of brightest light, not illumined at an appointed time.
problems.fix: The one who has chosen virtue resembles a man who sees each thing clearly and upward, his own course made in the season of brightest light.
problems.ruling: ἔοικε governs ὁ... βλέποντι ('resembles one looking upward'); 'looks clearly upward' drops the likeness, and πεποιημένῳ καιρῷ 'made in season of brightest light' is misrendered as 'illumined at appointed time'.
